html:
Early Dynastic Egypt was the first Egyptian state, formed when Upper and Lower Egypt were united around 3100 BCE, and it lasted through the First and Second Dynasties until about 2686 BCE. Dates this early can be off by a century or more.

Before it, the Nile valley in the south and the delta in the north had separate chiefdoms and cultures. Tradition credits a southern king, Narmer (perhaps the same person as the legendary Menes), with joining them. The Narmer Palette shows him wearing the crowns of both lands and striking an enemy.

What the early kings built:

  • A new capital at Memphis, at the point where the valley meets the delta, so the king could control both.
  • Royal tombs at Abydos, the old home of their line, and large mud-brick tombs for officials at Saqqara.
  • A royal administration that counted cattle, collected taxes and recorded the height of the Nile flood each year.
  • Hieroglyphic writing, which grew up in this period alongside the state.

The king was already shown as a god on earth, protected by the falcon god Horus. Many of the lasting features of Egyptian civilisation, from royal art to the idea of one land under one king, were set in these four centuries.

Egypt had trade contacts with Mesopotamia, where the Sumerian cities were growing at the same time. The period ends with the Third Dynasty, whose king Djoser built the first pyramid and opened the Old Kingdom.
